text: Austerity means strictness and self-denial, a life stripped of comforts and extras. In economics it names a deliberate government program of deep spending cuts, often with tax rises, to close the gap between what a country spends and what it collects. The article lists it among the painful options the US may face if growth alone can't ease its debt.

To outstrip something is to grow or move faster than it and pull ahead, the way a sprinter outstrips the pack. Here government spending has outstripped tax revenues: it grew faster, and the widening gap became borrowed money.

Fiscal describes anything to do with a government's budget, the taxes it collects and the money it spends. An economist in the article calls years of overspending "fiscally misbehaving". Its partner term is monetary, which covers interest rates and the money supply.

t: take your eye off the ball
forms: taking their eye off the ball
text: To take your eye off the ball is to stop paying attention to the thing that matters, like a fielder glancing away just as the ball arrives. The article suggests Americans, busy with celebrations and sport, may have stopped watching the economy.
Saying someone could be forgiven for doing something means their mistake is understandable, given the circumstances. It's a polite way of excusing people before pointing out what they missed.
News hits the headlines when it suddenly becomes a big story everyone is reporting. The debt had been climbing quietly for years; passing $40 trillion is what pushed it onto front pages.
A wake-up call is an event that jolts people into noticing a problem and acting on it, like an alarm going off. Reagan treated the first $1 trillion of debt in 1981 as exactly that kind of warning.
A line in the sand is a marker that says: past this point, things are serious. The $40 trillion milestone doesn't change anything by itself, but it's a visible boundary being crossed.

A fire sale is a panicked sell-off at almost any price, named for merchants dumping smoke-damaged goods after a fire. If investors ever lost faith in US bonds all at once, they'd rush to sell them cheap, and that panic is what economists fear.

British slang: at a fair lick means at a good, brisk speed. The US economy has slowed recently but is still growing at a decent pace, which matters because growth brings the tax revenue that pays the bills.
Something ballooning is swelling fast, inflating like a balloon. Costs for government programs didn't just rise, they ballooned, growing much quicker than the tax money meant to pay for them.
Revenue is the money coming in. For a business that's sales; for a government it's mostly taxes. The article's core problem in one line: spending grew faster than revenues.
To undermine something is to weaken it from below, like digging out the ground under a wall. Tax cuts undermined revenues: they quietly reduced the money coming in even as spending climbed.

A milestone is a marker of how far you've come, from the old stone posts placed every mile along roads. Round numbers like $1 trillion in 1981 or $40 trillion now don't change the economics, but they make people stop and take stock.
Wary means cautious and on guard, alert to possible danger. Investors are wary of the sheer size of US debt, so they want extra reward before lending more.

In investing, a return is what you earn back on the money you put in, usually given as a percentage. When the bond market demands higher returns, it means lenders insist on more interest before they'll buy government bonds.

An eye-watering amount is so large it almost makes your eyes water, shockingly big. Tech firms are borrowing eye-watering sums for AI, and that borrowing competes with the government for the same investors' cash.

Appetite here isn't about food: investor appetite is the desire to buy. When appetite for US bonds diminishes, fewer people want to lend to the government, so it must offer higher interest to tempt them.
Diminishing means shrinking, becoming steadily smaller. Investor willingness to lend to the US is diminishing, and that fading demand is what starts the vicious cycle the article describes.

A vicious cycle is a loop where each bad outcome causes the next: wary investors demand higher interest, higher interest makes the debt grow faster, faster-growing debt makes investors warier still. Once the loop starts, it feeds itself.
Critical here doesn't mean criticizing; it means at a crisis point, the way doctors say a patient is in critical condition. Economists say the US isn't there yet: a flashing yellow light, not red.

Emeritus is a title for a professor who has retired but keeps the rank as an honor, from Latin for "having earned one's discharge". Charlie Bean is an emeritus professor at the London School of Economics.
Turmoil is a state of wild confusion and disorder. Financial market turmoil means prices swinging violently and investors panicking, which is what a sudden loss of faith in US bonds could trigger.

A mortgage is the long-term loan a family takes to buy a home, paid back with interest over decades. When government borrowing pushes interest rates up, mortgage rates follow, so the debt problem lands on ordinary households.
Grim means bleak and worrying, with little to smile about. Add up the overspending, the borrowing and the higher interest rates, and the picture begins to look grim.
A surge is a sudden powerful rise, like a wave. Public spending surges under both Trump and Biden, especially during Covid, are a big part of how the debt doubled in a decade.

Borrowed from aviation: a longer runway means more room before you must take off or stop. Saying the US has a longer runway to misbehave means it can keep overborrowing longer than other countries before disaster forces a change.
Something short-lived lasts only briefly. The Treasury's bond buyback lowered borrowing costs for about a day before they bounced back up, a sign quick fixes aren't working.

Pocketbook is an old American word for a wallet or purse, so someone's pocketbook stands for their personal finances. Saying the debt finds its way to people's pocketbooks means ordinary families end up paying, through pricier loans and goods.
A problem spills over when it flows past its container and affects others, like an overfull glass. Higher US borrowing costs spill over into other countries, raising what they must pay to borrow too.
To buy back is to repurchase something you originally sold. The Treasury bought back some of its own bonds to boost demand for them, hoping to nudge borrowing costs down.

The worldwide marketplace where bonds, tradeable IOUs from governments and companies, are bought and sold. Its daily prices set what interest rates borrowers must pay, which gives it real power over even the US government.

The gap in a single year between what the government spends and what it collects in taxes. Not the same as the debt, which is all the past deficits piled up and still owed. See the handout's Debt vs. deficit card.

A legal limit Congress sets on how much the US government may borrow, currently $41.1 trillion. When debt nears the ceiling, Congress must raise it or the government risks running out of borrowing room.
The nonpartisan agency that does budget math for Congress, forecasting spending, revenue and debt. It's the source of the projection that US debt will hit about $64 trillion by 2036.

The currency the world's central banks and traders hold and use for international business, which today is the US dollar. Constant global demand for dollars means constant demand for US bonds, letting America borrow more cheaply and for longer than anyone else.

The Group of Seven, a club of big wealthy democracies: the US, UK, Japan, Germany, France, Italy and Canada. Among them, Japan and Italy carry even more debt relative to their economies than the US does.
America's central bank, which sets short-term interest rates and watches over the financial system. One of the article's experts, Eric Swanson, used to be a senior economist there.
The branch of the US government that manages the nation's money: collecting taxes, paying bills and, crucially here, borrowing by selling government bonds.

Literally the president's residence, but in news writing it stands for the president and their administration. Saying the White House wants to deliver on the economy means the president's team wants voters to see results.
US congressional elections held halfway through a president's four-year term. They're read as a report card on the administration, which is why economic worries loom large right before them.

Clever technical maneuvers with money designed to improve how the numbers look without fixing the underlying problem. The article uses it a bit dismissively for the Treasury's bond buyback: a tweak, not a cure.

Renegotiating what a borrower owes, by stretching out payments, lowering the interest, or paying back less than promised. For a country it's a drastic, trust-burning step, which is why it sits last on the article's list of options.

A general rise in prices that makes each dollar buy less. Recent inflation shocks pushed interest rates up, and those higher rates are what suddenly made carrying $40 trillion of debt so much more expensive.

Government spending that supports people directly, like Social Security pensions and health coverage such as Medicare. These are the biggest and fastest-growing pieces of the US budget. British spelling: programmes.
